questions.q: What are the three parts of a JWT?
o: Header, payload (claims) and signature
Key, value and checksum
Token, secret and expiry
Issuer, subject and password
questions.w: The parts are Base64URL encoded and joined by dots. The header names the algorithm and the payload holds the claims.

questions.q: Is the payload of a normal signed JWT (JWS) secret?
o: No, it is only encoded, so anyone with the token can read it
Yes, it is encrypted with the signing key
Yes, but only while sent over HTTPS
No, because it is always empty by design
questions.w: Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality. Never put secrets or sensitive personal data in claims, or use JWE for encryption.

questions.q: What does the signature let a resource server verify?
o: That a trusted party issued it and nobody has altered it
That the user is still logged in right now
That the user's password is still correct
That the token has never been used before
questions.w: The server verifies the signature with a shared secret (HS256) or the issuer's public key (RS256, ES256). It does not know if the token was revoked.

questions.q: Which claims should a resource server always validate?
o: Signature, `exp`, `iss` and `aud`
Only the signature, nothing more
Only the user name inside the token
Only the total length of the token
questions.w: An expired, wrongly-issued or wrongly-targeted token must be rejected even if the signature is valid. Pin the accepted algorithms too.

questions.q: A JWT header says `"alg": "none"`. How should a secure server react?
o: Reject it, since only the expected algorithms are accepted
Accept it, because no signature means no risk
Accept it when the caller is an internal user
Switch to HS256 automatically and carry on
questions.w: The `alg=none` and RS256-to-HS256 confusion attacks come from trusting the algorithm named in the token. Configure it on the server.

questions.q: Where is the safest place for a browser app to keep a long-lived refresh token?
o: An `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie
`localStorage` in the browser
A global JavaScript variable
The URL query string
questions.w: Script-readable storage can be stolen by XSS. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by JavaScript, though you must then defend against CSRF.

questions.q: Why are access tokens kept short-lived (minutes) and paired with a refresh token?
o: A stolen access token expires fast, and refresh tokens can be revoked
Short tokens are cheaper for the server to sign than long ones
Browsers automatically delete any token that lives too long
Refresh tokens are never kept anywhere on a server
questions.w: Stateless JWTs cannot be revoked easily. A short lifetime limits exposure and the refresh flow gives the server a revocation point.

questions.q: When might you prefer an opaque session id over a JWT?
o: You need instant revocation and server-side control of sessions
You want the system to keep no server state of any kind
Every client must be able to read the claims itself
The credential has to be larger than a normal token
questions.w: JWTs are great for stateless APIs between services. Server sessions revoke instantly, but need shared storage when scaled out.
